Section One: The Origin of the Dharma Assembly (The assembly for preaching the Dharma originated from this).

Thus have I heard: At one time the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park, together with a great community of bhikṣus, numbering one thousand two hundred and fifty persons.
At that time, when it was mealtime, the World-Honored One put on his robes, took up his bowl, and entered [the city].
He went for alms in the great city of Śrāvastī. Having finished his sequential begging within the city, he returned to his original place.

When he had finished eating, he put away his robes and bowl, washed his feet, arranged his seat, and sat down. (The pronunciation of *zhe* [in *zhuzuo*] is like *zhuo*; the pronunciation of *bo* [in *bō*] is like *bo*; the pronunciation of *fànshí* is like *fǎnsì*).
[Note] "Thus" refers to the entire sutra. "I" is Ānanda’s self-designation, stating that what is spoken in this sutra was personally heard by him from the Buddha.
"Buddha" is a title for the Teacher. Śrāvastī is the capital where King Prasenajit resided.
As for the "tree," it was planted by Jeta, the crown prince of King Prasenajit; therefore, it is called "Jeta’s Grove. [The place where] the offerings were provided...
There was a man named Sudatta who delighted in goodness and loved to give alms; everyone called him the Elder Anāthapiṇḍada.
Sudatta held the Buddha’s teachings in profound reverence and borrowed a garden from Jeta to construct a vihāra, covering the ground with gold.
He requested the Buddha to preach the Dharma; therefore, the Buddha constantly dwelt within the garden. "Bhikṣu" refers to a mendicant:

one who, above, begs the Dharma from the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, and below, begs for food from the faithful. "World-Honored One" (*Sezun*) is a title for the Buddha, signifying that he is venerated by all within the three realms.
"Fū" (to spread) means to arrange or lay out.

[The Narrator] said: Ānanda spoke thus: "I have previously heard that our Buddha, the Tathāgata, was once staying in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park, in the kingdom of Śrāvastī, with one thousand two hundred and fifty bhikṣus seated beneath him."
At that time, it was exactly midday. Just as they were about to take their meal, the Buddha donned his robes of gentle forbearance and took the alms bowl offered by the Four Heavenly Kings.
Leading the great assembly, he entered the city of Śrāvastī to beg for food.

He did not bypass the poor to seek the wealthy, nor did he abandon the lowly to follow the noble; he proceeded with impartiality and without distinction. Having completed his sequential begging, he returned.
He returned to the grove. Having finished his meal, he put away his robe and bowl, washed his feet, arranged the high seat, and sat upon it.

[They] have set their minds on *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. How should they abide? How should they subdue their minds?
The Buddha said: "Excellent, excellent, Subhūti! It is as you have said. The Tathāgata well protects and sustains all bodhisattvas;

**Chapter Three: The Section on the True Source of the Mahāyāna** (The Greatest Vehicle and the Most Authentic Doctrine) The Buddha addressed Subhūti:
"All bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should subdue their minds in this manner. Whatever..."
Of all classes of sentient beings—whether born from eggs, born from wombs, born from moisture, or born by transformation; whether possessing form or formless;
whether with perception, without perception, or neither with nor without perception—I shall cause them all to enter *nirvāṇa* without remainder and bring them to liberation.
In this way, I shall liberate immeasurable, incalculable, and boundless multitudes of beings.
"Subhūti, in truth, there are no sentient beings who attain parinirvāṇa. Why is this?

Subhūti, if a bodhisattva possesses the notion of a self, the notion of a person, the notion of a sentient being, or the notion of a life-span, then he is not a bodhisattva. (The word "nirvāṇa" is pronounced *kǎnpán*.)
[Note] *Mahāsattva* is a Sanskrit term; in the language of China, it means "the essence of the mind is vast and immeasurable.
*Andaja* refers to birds born from eggs. *Jarāyuja* refers to humans and beasts born from a womb. *Saṃsvedaja* refers to scaly creatures born from moisture within the water.
*Upapāduka* (birth by transformation) refers to species such as flies and mosquitoes. *Rūpin* (possessing form) means having only physical form and sound, but lacking desire and lust.

*Arūpin* (formless) means possessing only the spiritual consciousness (*vijñāna*) but lacking a physical body. *Sañjñin* (possessing perception) means that within the mind there is still calculation and deliberation.
*Asañjñin* (without perception) means silently encompassing all phenomena with a single thought unmoving. *Naiva-sañjñin-na-asañjñin* (neither with nor without perception)...
It is without conceptualization (*asaṃjñā*). Although not a single thought moves, it is not like wood or stone that lack cognition.
As for the latter five [realms], they are all inhabitants of the heavens; there is nothing else beyond them. *Nir* means non-arising; *vāṇa* means non-dying.
"Parinirvāṇa" means to extinguish all marks and thereby deliver beings through transformation.
[Commentary] When Subhūti heard what the Buddha had said, his mind was opened and enlightened. Thereupon, the Buddha spoke to him again, saying:
Subhūti, since the nature and capacity of all bodhisattvas are vast and great, they should subdue their minds in this manner.

This being so, my own mind is the very mind of all beings; it is the mind of every class of sentient being—whether born from eggs, born from wombs, born from moisture, or born by transformation; whether belonging to the heavens, possessing form or being formless, or possessing perception.
Neither non-perception, nor perception, nor the absence of perception. Although their categories differ and their levels of realization vary, I cause them all to be neither born nor to die;
I extinguish their various marks and deliver them, causing them likewise to subdue their own minds.
Thus, they are immeasurable, countless, and boundless in their realms.
All these sentient beings have been brought to parinirvāṇa; yet this is the self-extinction and self-deliverance of the beings themselves—what merit do I possess therein?

Why is this so? For if the parinirvāṇa of sentient beings were attributed to my merit, this mind would then have something upon which it clings, and one could not avoid the burden of the four marks [of self, person, being, and life]. This is like a mind that clings to greed.
If the mind clings to one extreme of anger, it discriminates between "you" and "I," giving rise to the mark of a person (*pudgala-nimitta*).

If the mind clings to one extreme of delusion, it aspires to be born among the devas, giving rise to the mark of a sentient being (*sattva-nimitta*). If the mind clings to one extreme of craving, it hopes for long life, giving rise to the mark of a life-span possessor (*jīvaka-nimitta*).
If the mind clings to one extreme of attachment, it regards things as its own, calculating private interests and giving rise to the mark of a self (*ātman-nimitta*).
If one possesses these four characteristics, can they still be called a bodhisattva?
**Chapter Four: Sublime Practice Without Abiding** (The profound and sublime practice is fundamentally without attachment or dwelling.
Furthermore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva should practice giving without abiding in any phenomenon. That is to say, not...

[Note]: Furthermore, this refers to the re-arrangement of the dialogue between the Buddha and Subhūti.

Regarding the "Dharma of the Dharma of the Bodhisattva," it refers to that which is employed and applied by the mind and body in their responsive interactions. "Abiding" (sthiti) means to grasp or adhere to.

"Adorning" means to bestow. "To spread" means to distribute universally. "Giving" means to disperse. "Form" refers to physical appearance; "sound" refers to music; "fragrance" refers to the scent of aromatic incense.
Taste refers to varieties of cooked and roasted foods. Touch means movement; some say it also includes sexual desire between men and women.
Dharma refers to the principles governing things and phenomena. Since all dharmas arise conditioned by the mind, they are subsumed under the faculty of mind.
[Commentary] The Buddha, continuing from the meaning of signlessness (*animitta*), again addressed Subhūti, saying:
"In all the mental activities of a bodhisattva and in all the physical responses of his person, he should remain entirely without dwelling or attachment;
this is especially true in the case of giving (*dāna*). Why is this? When ordinary people practice giving, they often seek after personal benefit, as if [looking with] their eyes..."
Regarding forms, sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, and mental objects:
if even one of these does not accord with one's desires, one will inevitably practice giving in order to satisfy those desires.
This is giving while dwelling upon signs. When a bodhisattva’s six sense faculties are pure and free from all seeking for desires, they give only through the Dharma to benefit all sentient beings.
Like water within the earth, they act without doing anything at all; this is what is called "giving while not dwelling upon signs.
Subhūti, a bodhisattva’s giving must necessarily be like this, without the six... [signs].
Only when one is free from the burden of worldly dust is it true giving; only then does one obtain great benefit.
Why is this so? It is because material giving pertains to the mundane, while the gift of Dharma pertains to the sacred.

When a Bodhisattva practices giving without abiding in signs and without a heart of expectation, they transcend the suffering of birth and death to receive great bliss that remains undestroyed throughout ten thousand kalpas, surpassing the three realms.
It endures for a long time. Although its merit is great, one should also allow it to be as it is;
it is truly beyond thought or calculation. For once it is subjected to deliberation, this mind dwells upon signs (*nimitta*), and the merit, conversely, becomes small.
"Indeed, merit and virtue are truly beyond measure; yet even to attempt to measure them is of no benefit. I shall ask you this:
the empty space of the eastern direction may be said to be vast. Do you measure it?
Subhūti replied, "As for such places of empty space, what use is there in imagining them? I do not measure them. The Buddha spoke again: "The southern, western, and northern directions..."
"The four intermediate directions, above, and below—the void—is even greater. Do you contemplate this?
Subhūti replied, "Regarding these spaces of the void, even to attempt to conceive of them is useless; I do not contemplate them.
The Buddha said, "If you know that the void cannot be contemplated, then you shall know the merit of a bodhisattva’s giving without abiding in signs."
It is also like empty space; it is utterly beyond the reach of thought or calculation. You need only rely upon my teaching:
if the mind abides in the signless, you will spontaneously attain transcendental realization.
Chapter Five: Seeing According to Reality (Seeing the True Reality by Means of the Principle of Suchness).
Subhūti, what do you think? Can the Tathāgata be seen by means of physical marks? “No, World-Honored One;
the Tathāgata cannot be seen by means of physical marks. Why is this? The physical marks spoken of by the Tathāgata are not, in fact, physical marks.
[The Buddha said: "Subhūti, all marks whatsoever are empty and false. If one perceives that all marks are no-marks, then one sees the Tathāgata.
[Note: "What do you think? is a phrase used to pose a question. "Physical marks" refers to the currently manifest physical body (*rūpakāya*). "Perceives" means...
"Look! This is not the seeing that perceives marks.
[Commentary] The Buddha said to Subhūti: "If you know that merit cannot be measured, then it is clear that giving should not abide in marks.
Is this true only of giving? It is also true of this very form I now manifest."
The body, too, is not real. Allow me to ask you this: can one take this physical body composed of the four great elements and say that the Tathāgata is present therein?
Subhūti replied: "A physical body is but a collection of skeletal remains; such a Buddha would be no different from an ordinary person.
It is truly impossible to perceive the Tathāgata through bodily marks. Why is this? Because the Buddha takes the Dharma as his body."
Pure and utterly pristine, like the great void that does not cling to forms or traces. Although it possesses the marks of a body, in reality it has no marks of a body.
The "marks of the body" spoken of by the Tathāgata now are the Dharma-body, not the form-body (*rūpakāya*).
One may perceive the Tathāgata through the Dharma-body; how could one perceive the Tathāgata through the form-body? The Buddha said, "Subhūti, as for what you have said..."
It is so. All marks possessed by ordinary people belong to the realm of the false and illusory. Being illusory, they are unreal;
being false, they are not true. To seek to see the Tathāgata through such unreal and untrue marks is like mistaking an external enemy for a family member—it can never come to pass.
If a person can perceive that all marks are non-marks, then within the physical body, they will see...
The Dharma-body; therein the Tathāgata resides. Chapter Six:
The Rarity of Right Faith (In which it is most rare for one to give rise to right faith).
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying: “World-Honored One, are there any sentient beings who, upon hearing such spoken words and phrases as these, [will attain right faith]?”
“Do they give rise to true faith? The Buddha told Subhūti: “Do not speak thus.

After the parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata, during the final five hundred years, there will be those who uphold the precepts and cultivate merit who are able to give rise to faith in these chapters and verses, regarding them as true.
You should know that such persons have planted roots of goodness not under one, two, three, four, or five Buddhas alone, but have already [done so] under countless Buddhas.”

Subhūti, those who have approached as many as ten million buddhas, planted various roots of goodness, and upon hearing these phrases, give rise to even a single thought of pure faith—in all such beings, the Tathāgata fully knows and fully sees that they shall obtain such immeasurable merit. Why is this?
Because these beings no longer possess the notion of a self, the notion of a person, the notion of a sentient being, or the notion of a life-span.

There is no mark of dharmas, nor is there any mark of non-dharmas. Why is this? If these sentient beings take up marks with their minds, they immediately become attached to a self, a person, a sentient being, and a life-span.
If they take up the mark of dharmas, they likewise become attached to a self, a person, a sentient being, and a life-span.
Why is this? If one grasps at the marks of what is not the Dharma, one is immediately attached to a self, a person, a sentient being, or a life-span.
Therefore, one should not grasp at the Dharma, nor should one grasp at what is not the Dharma. For this reason, the Tathāgata has always said to you bhikṣus:
"Understand my teaching of the Dharma as being like the parable of the raft. Even the Dharma should be relinquished, let alone what is not the Dharma."
[Note] These words and phrases refer to the preceding chapters. The expression "five hundred years" is a term used to indicate a vast distance of time.
"Observing the precepts" means: "Commit no evil. "Cultivating merit" means: "Perform all good deeds.
To take this as reality is to have firm conviction without doubt. "Planting roots of goodness" refers precisely to the meaning of observing the precepts and cultivating merit. This is pure faith.
This means that one should have faith because the mind is constantly pure. The Tathāgata knows all and sees all; the mind is united with the Buddha, and the Buddha is united with the mind.
There is no mark of dharmas, for the myriad dharmas are all empty. There is no mark of non-dharmas, for external conditions are entirely pure.
When the Tathāgata frequently says "thus," it is because former Buddhas had these words, and the Buddha now recounts them.
"Raft" (*phalaka*) means a boat. "Metaphor" (*upamā*) means a comparison. The Buddha-dharma’s salvation of sentient beings is compared to crossing people over water by boat. [Commentary:
Subhūti feared that after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, there would be no one to transmit the Dharma, and that future sentient beings would be unable to give rise to faith;
therefore, he addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, with a heart of great compassion, you have composed this rare discourse. Among those seated here..."

"All the bhikṣus will surely revere and uphold it. However, after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, as for future sentient beings who hear such words and phrases, do you not know whether they too can give rise to a heart of true faith?
The Buddha said, "Subhūti, the essence of nature is eternally luminous and the lamp of the mind does not extinguish. You must not speak in this way. For..."
These spoken words and phrases are most subtle and most wondrous.

Even during the period of more than five hundred years after the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa, there were still those who maintained the pure precepts and cultivated celestial merit, regarding these as the true and sublime truth.

As for those who possess firm and unshakable conviction: since they are able to maintain such firm conviction more than five hundred years after [the Buddha's passing], their roots of goodness must have been planted more than five hundred years prior.
You should know that such persons did not plant these roots of goodness under only one, two, three, four, or five Buddhas;
rather, they have already planted them in the presence of immeasurable thousands of millions of Buddhas.
They have planted various roots of goodness; they have seen many Buddhas, heard much of the Dharma, and practiced extensively.

Not only are the roots of goodness of those who uphold the precepts and cultivate merit beyond measure, but even if worldly beings hear these phrases and give rise to pure faith for even a single moment, this mind immediately merges with that of the Tathāgata, as if receiving it directly from him.
It is taught that it is just as with the Tathāgata; the Tathāgata’s Buddha-wisdom and Buddha-eye know them all and see them all.
The merit obtained by these sentient beings is likewise immeasurable. Why is this so?

It is because they have already attained the wondrous meaning of the twofold emptiness of phenomena and persons. Although these sentient beings may possess only a single moment of pure faith, [the merit is immeasurable].
Yet in this single thought-moment, there is no longer any mark of a self, mark of a person, mark of a sentient being, or mark of a life-span;

this is the emptiness of beings (*pudgala-śūnyatā*). There is no mark of dharmas, nor any mark of non-dharmas; this is the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*). These are the two emptinesses of beings and phenomena.
What is the meaning of this? It is, essentially, not to cling to signs. If these sentient beings allow their minds to grasp at signs, they immediately give rise to attachment;
they then become attached to the notions of self, person, sentient being, and life-span. If they grasp at the signs of dharmas, they immediately engage in the adherence to dharmas;

they then become attached to the notions of self, person, sentient being, and life-span. If they grasp at the signs of non-dharmas, this likewise constitutes adherence to dharmas, and they likewise become attached to the notions of self... [and so forth].
Regarding persons, sentient beings, living souls, and individuals, the characteristic of arising is certainly not to be grasped; likewise, neither phenomena nor non-phenomena should be grasped.
Therefore, those who uphold the precepts and cultivate merit must cause this mind to be empty, void, and hollow, such that not a single thing exists within it.
They should not grasp at the marks of phenomena, nor should they grasp at the marks of non-phenomena. Such is the principle of this teaching.
It is most subtle and wondrous. Therefore, the Tathāgatas of old have often said to the great assembly:
"O bhikṣus, you should know that I use the Dharma to deliver people, just as one uses a raft to cross over water. Once people have reached the shore, the raft is no longer needed;
when a person can attain full realization, the Dharma is likewise of no further use. Viewed from this perspective, even the Dharma should be relinquished.
How much more so for non-Buddhist outsiders who follow what is not the Dharma?
Chapter Seven: Neither Attainment nor Exposition (Emptiness entails no attainment; quiescence entails no exposition).
Subhūti, what do you think? Has the Tathāgata attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*?

"Has the Tathāgata preached any Dharma? Subhūti replied, "As I understand the meaning of what the Buddha has preached, there is no fixed dharma called 'Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi,' nor is there any fixed dharma that the Tathāgata can preach. Why is this?
All dharmas preached by the Tathāgata are ungraspable and inexpressible; they are neither dharmas nor non-dharmas."
The Dharma. Why is this? All worthy sages and saints are distinguished by means of the unconditioned dharma (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*).
[Note: "Has one attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*? means that one has thoroughly realized emptiness;
there is no fixed dharma to be attained. "Is there any dharma taught? means that teaching is given according to people; there is no fixed dharma to be taught.
It cannot be grasped; it cannot be grasped by means of physical form. It cannot be spoken; it cannot be spoken with the mouth and tongue.

It is not a dharma; though it exists, it is yet non-existent. It is not a non-dharma; though it does not exist, it is yet existent. In all cases, the character "yi" (以) is to be understood as the character "zuoyong" (作用), meaning "function" or "activity."
【Lecture】 The Buddha told Subhūti: "In my teaching, unsurpassed bodhi is indeed the primary goal.
Nevertheless, it may be attained through the observance of precepts, or it may be attained through meditative concentration; thus, the methods of practice differ."
The results obtained are each distinct. Do you therefore think that there is a fixed dharma to be attained by the Tathāgata regarding unsurpassed bodhi?
The gate of the Buddha is vast; indeed, he does not select people before teaching them.
Nevertheless, he speaks deeply with the wise and speaks superficially with the foolish. Since their innate capacities are not uniform, the instructions bestowed upon them also differ. As for you—
[Subhūti] thought: "Does the Tathāgata have a fixed dharma that can be taught? Subhūti replied:
"As I understand the meaning of what the Buddha has taught, I know that the Buddha cultivated himself through the meaning of unsurpassed bodhi;
there is no fixed dharma that can be named. He teaches others through the meaning of unsurpassed bodhi, and likewise there is no fixed [dharma]."

The Dharma can be spoken. Why is this? The Dharma taught by the Tathāgata can be cultivated through its essential nature (*dharmatā*), yet it cannot be grasped through physical characteristics (*rūpa-lakṣaṇa*).
It can be realized through the mind, yet it cannot be expressed by the tongue or mouth.

If one considers it to be a "Dharma that exists," although it exists, it does not stagnate in existence. If one considers it to be a "Dharma that does not exist," although it is non-existent, it is not discussed as such.
Regarding "non-existence": this is why no fixed dharma can be found. Why is this so? Because dharmas are fundamentally unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
Since antiquity, the sages and worthies have all used the dharma of non-action to instruct people; yet those of shallow capacity perceive only what is shallow.
Those who see deeply see the deep; there cannot but be distinctions. This is why there is no single, fixed dharma that can be taught.
Section Eight: Arising in Accordance with the Dharma (The dharmas of all Buddhas arise in accordance with this).

"Subhūti, what do you think? If someone were to fill a trichiliocosm with the seven treasures and give them as a gift, would the merit obtained by that person be great? Subhūti replied, "It would be very great, World-Honored One."
Why is this? Because that merit is not the nature of merit; therefore, the Tathāgata says it is much merit.
Furthermore, Subhūti, if there is someone who receives, upholds, and even recites as few as four lines of verse from this sutra for others, their merit shall surpass that.
Why is this? Subhūti, all Buddhas and the unsurpassed...
The Dharma of *samyak-saṃbodhi* all issues from this sutra. Subhūti, what is called the Buddha-dharma is not, in fact, Buddha-dharma.
(The rhyme for "dharma" is *ji*.)
[Note] That which lies beneath the entire sky is called a small world (*sāhasracūḍika-lokadhātu*). One thousand small worlds are called a small thousand (*sāhasra*).
One thousand small thousands are called a middle thousand (*dvisāhasramadhyama*). One thousand middle thousands are called a great thousand (*trisāhasramahāsāhasra*).
In reality, it is one single great thousand; this constitutes the trichiliocosm (*trisāhasramahāsāhasralokadhātu*). The seven treasures: lapis lazuli (*vaiḍūrya*).
Crystal, pearls, agate, coral, gold, silver, and merit—by cultivating the virtue of giving, one enjoys blessings in the present life.
As for the nature of merit: by cultivating the virtuous nature within the nature itself, it pervades the six directions; the receiving of such blessings is likewise so.
The four-line verse should be understood as referring to the absence of the mark of self, the mark of person, the mark of sentient being, and the mark of a life-span.
Only then will there be a definitive conclusion. As for the claim that this verse need not be explained in detail, it appears to be merely empty and superficial, and thus cannot be followed.
[Commentary] Previously, it was stated that dharmas are unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*). The Buddha’s intention was to manifest the merit of the unconditioned;
therefore, he first discussed with him the merit that is subject to exhaustion. Consequently, he posed a question, saying: "Subhūti, what do you think? If there were a person..."
"In this regard, if one were to use the seven treasures of a trichiliocosm as an act of giving, would the merit obtained by that person be great?
Subhūti replied, "When ordinary people practice giving, they originally desire to seek benefit;
how could they not wish for their merit to be great? However, what they obtain is merely external to the self."
This is merit, but it is not the merit inherent in one's nature. Why is this?

Accumulating wealth to practice giving is merely cultivating virtue by borrowing external objects; since such objects are finite, the resulting merit is also finite and cannot be compared to the merit inherent in one's nature.
Nevertheless, the Tathāgata repeatedly inquires about the merit of such a person because—
Although what they have attained is much, it can still be calculated by number. The Buddha said, "Subhūti, what you say is indeed true.
To cultivate by relying on external things is not as good as cultivating by following one's own nature. And the method for cultivating this nature does not lie outside this sutra.
Furthermore, if there be another person who receives this sutra and keeps it in mind without forgetting, and upholds it..."
Without wearying of its duration, one should even expound as little as a four-line verse for others.
Not only does this awaken the nature of oneself alone, but it shall also awaken the nature of hundreds of millions of people.
Is its merit not surely superior to the merit of that [previous] giving? Why is this? Because this sutra is the path of practice; for anyone who...
All Buddhas and the dharmas of the unsurpassed bodhi of all Buddhas all emerge from this.
Now, the dharma of unsurpassed bodhi is precisely the Buddha-dharma; yet how could the Buddha-dharma be clung to as something fixed? That which is called "Buddha-dharma" originally does not exist;
it is merely a provisional means used to awaken sentient beings. How could there be anything truly real?
The Buddha-dharma! Chapter Nine:
The Section on One Mark and No-Mark (This single mark is fundamentally formless from the beginning).
Subhūti, what do you think? Does a srotāpanna have the thought, "I have attained the fruit of srotāpanna"?
"No. Subhūti said, "No indeed, World-Honored One. Why is this? A *srotāpanna* is called 'one who has entered the stream,' yet there is nothing entered;
they do not enter into form, sound, smell, taste, touch, or dharmas. This is called a *srotāpanna*. Subhūti, what do you think?
Does a *sakṛdāgāmin* have the thought, 'I have attained the fruit of a *sakṛdāgāmin*'? Subhūti...
He replied, “No, World-Honored One. Why is this? A *sakṛdāgāmin* is called ‘one who comes back once,’ yet in reality there is no coming or going;
it is for this reason that he is called a *sakṛdāgāmin*. Subhūti, what do you think?
Does an *anāgāmin* have the thought, ‘I have attained the fruit of *anāgāmin*’? Subhūti said, “No, World-Honored One. Why is this? An *anāgāmin*...”
"He is called 'One Who Does Not Return' (Anāgāmin), yet in reality there is no such thing as 'not returning. Therefore he is named Anāgāmin.
"Subhūti, what do you think? Can an Arhat have the thought: 'I have attained the path of Arhatship'? Subhūti replied:
"No, World-Honored One. Why is this? Truly, there is no dharma that can be called 'Arhat.
World-Honored One, if an Arhat were to have the thought, 'I have attained the path of an Arhat,' he would thereby be attached to a self, a person, a sentient being, or a life-span.
World-Honored One, the Buddha has said of me: 'Among men, I am the foremost of those who possess the Samādhi of Non-contention; I am the foremost of those free from desire.'"
“Arhat! World-Honored One, I do not harbor such a thought as ‘I am an Arhat free from desire.
World-Honored One, if I were to harbor such a thought as ‘I have attained the path of Arhatship,’ then the World-Honored One would not say that Subhūti is one who delights in the practice of araṇā.
This is because, Subhūti, in reality there is nothing practiced, yet he is named Subhūti; thus he is one who delights [in araṇā].”
Araṇa-vihārin (the first character *huán* pronounced as *wán*, the second character *nà* pronounced as *nú*).

[Note] To be able to form such a thought refers to the initial sprouting of the aspiration for attaining the Way. The four preceding instances of the word "I" (*wo*) are terms used to represent the conceptualizations of the *srotāpanna* and others;
they are not the Buddha’s own self-designation. The Sanskrit term is *srotāpanna*; in Chinese...
"Srotāpanna" (Stream-enterer) refers to the first person who has truly entered the stream. "Sakṛdāgāmin" in Sanskrit means "Once-returner" in Chinese;
this refers to one who dwells once more in the heavens of the form realm before entering the human world for one final birth. "Anāgāmin" in Sanskrit means "Non-returner" in Chinese;
this refers to one who does not return to receive rebirth in the desire realm. "Arhat" in Sanskrit means "Worthy of Offerings" or "One of No-birth" in Chinese; this refers to...
The cessation of characteristics is the exhaustion of birth; it is non-contention (*araṇā*). It is entirely free from any intent to dispute.
"Samādhi" in Sanskrit means "right view" (*samyagdṛṣṭi*) in Chinese, meaning that one has distanced oneself from false views. "Joy" (*sukha*) means "delight. *Araṇa* is precisely non-contention.
The phrase "one who delights in the practice of *araṇa*" refers to a statement made by the Buddha, which Subhūti cites here as scriptural evidence.
[Commentary] The preceding discussion stated that the Dharma of non-action (wuwei) cannot be grasped and cannot be spoken.

Thus, when all Bodhisattvas practice, they should take non-thought (wunian) as their primary principle and must not harbor a mind seeking to attain the fruit [of enlightenment]. Therefore, the Buddha poses this question.
He said: "In my teaching to the great assembly, there are approximately four grades for those who cultivate the path of the Arhat:
namely, the Srotāpanna, the Sakṛdāgāmin, the Anāgāmin, and the Arhat. Their application of effort differs, and the fruits they attain likewise differ.
Subhūti, what do you think? When a Srotāpanna is practicing, if he were to..."
"If one forms the thought that they have attained the fruit, would they then truly attain the fruit of Srotāpanna? Subhūti replied, "No, World-Honored One.
Why is this? A Srotāpanna has entered the ranks of the noble ones and is thus called 'one who has entered the stream.

Yet, in their mind, there is nothing to be attained, and they do not cling to the characteristics of having entered the stream. They do not enter into the six sense bases of form, sound, smell, taste, touch, or dharmas."
Regarding the realm of sensory objects, one is called a *srotāpanna*. [The interlocutor] asks: "By what means is this granted? The Buddha said: "Subhūti, what do you think?
When a *sakṛdāgāmin* is practicing, if they were to pre-conceive the thought of attaining the fruit, would they then attain the fruit of a *sakṛdāgāmin*?
Subhūti replied: "No, World-Honored One. Why is that? Because a *sakṛdāgāmin*..."
The physical body goes once to the heavens and returns once to the human realm.

Although it is said that there is one going and one coming, the mind attains nothing and does not cling to the signs of arising and ceasing; in reality, there is no going or coming. This is called a Sakṛdāgāmin (Once-returner).
[The interlocutor] asked: "Is it because of this [that one attains the fruit]? The Buddha said: "Subhūti, what do you think?
When an Anāgāmin is practicing, if he were to pre-emptively form the thought of having attained the fruit, would he then attain the fruit of Anāgāmin?
Subhūti replied: "No, World-Honored One. Why is this? Because for an Anāgāmin, there is no desire in the internal mind and no desire in external objects."
One who does not return to take birth in this world is called an Anāgāmin (Non-returner). Yet, their mind attains nothing and they do not cling to the mark of non-returning;
this is termed an Anāgāmin. By means of this, the Buddha said: "Subhūti, what do you think?
When an Arhat is practicing, if they were to pre-conceive the thought of attaining the fruit, would they then attain Arhatship?"
"Is there not the path of the Arhat? Subhūti replied, "No, World-Honored One. Why is this?
For the Arhat, all conditions are entirely purified; there are no afflictions to be severed, no greed or hatred to be abandoned, and no mind that seeks to attain a fruit."
Since there is no mind that seeks to attain a fruit, there is no path to be attained and no dharma to be named;

this is what is called an Arhat. It is for this reason, World-Honored One. If these four kinds of Arhats should even slightly give rise to the thought of attainment within their minds, saying, "My practice can lead to the realization of the Arhat path," they immediately become attached to a self and persons.
If sentient beings still possess the four marks of a self and a life-span, can they truly be called Arhats?
It was just as when my disciples were permitted by the Buddha on that day to be called "transgressors.

To have no rivalry with others and no conflict with things, to remain far removed from false views, and to attain the Samādhi of Non-contention—this is extremely rare among the great assembly; it is the foremost.
"O World-Honored One, the reason you have designated me as the foremost among those Arhats who are free from desire is that I harbor no thought of attaining such a fruit.
Had I entertained even the slightest thought of attaining such a fruit,"
"If I were to think, 'I have attained the path of Arhatship,' then this mind would become attached to something.
The World-Honored One would not have called me one who delights in the practice of araṇā.
It is because I delight in the practice of araṇā while actually practicing nothing at all that the Buddha deeply accords with me and names me 'one who delights in the practice of araṇā.'"
Therefore, for all who wish to attain the fruit [of enlightenment], should they not eliminate the mind that seeks to "attain" it?
Section Ten: Adorning the Pure Land (Accomplishing the Adornment of the Pure and Radiant Mind-Ground).
The Buddha addressed Subhūti: "What do you think? When the Tathāgata was formerly with the Buddha Dīpaṃkara, did he have any [grasping] regarding dharmas?"
“Did you obtain anything? “No, World-Honored One. While I was with the Tathāgata Dīpaṃkara, I truly obtained nothing regarding the Dharma.
“Subhūti, what do you think? Does a bodhisattva adorn buddha-fields? “No, World-Honored One. Why is that?
That which is called ‘adorning a buddha-field’ is not actually adorning; it is merely named ‘adorning. Therefore, Subhūti, all [bodhisattvas]...”
Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should give rise to a pure mind in this way: they should not give rise to a mind dwelling on forms;
they should not give rise to a mind dwelling on sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, or dharmas. They should give rise to that mind with no dwelling-place.
Subhūti, suppose there were a person whose body was as large as Sumeru, the king of mountains. What do you think? Would that body be great? Subhūti...
"Venerable One, what you have said is truly great. Why is this? The Buddha has taught that 'non-body' is what is called the 'Great Body. [Note:
"Tathāgata" is a title by which the Buddha refers to himself. Dīpaṃkara Buddha was the teacher who conferred the prophecy upon Śākyamuni.

Since there must be one Buddha manifesting his transformation in every great world-system, it is said that the adornments of the Buddha-fields are like those produced by copying scriptures or creating images.]
Temples, offerings, almsgiving, and the like—therefore, Subhūti, these are general designations for all bodhisattvas.
"One should give rise to the mind by dwelling nowhere" means that the mind should dwell in the state of non-dwelling.
Mount Sumeru is three million three hundred and thirty-six thousand li in height and breadth; it is the king of all mountains.
It is not the physical body, but the Dharma-body—the true mind that is suchness and immovable.
[Commentary: Previously, Subhūti himself stated that regarding the fruit he had realized, he no longer harbored any thought of attainment.
The Buddha, fearing at last that his mind of attainment might not yet be exhausted, further enlightened him, saying: "Subhūti!"
"What do you think? Do you consider that when I was with the Buddha Dīpaṃkara and received my prediction, there was anything at all attained regarding the Dharma?
Subhūti replied, "No, World-Honored One. The Tathāgata’s mind is pure and serene;
although he received his prediction from the Buddha Dīpaṃkara, in reality, there was nothing at all attained regarding the Dharma. The Buddha said, "In one great world-system..."
Since there must be a Buddha who establishes transformation therein, it is called a "Buddha-field. [The questioner] asks:
"Do you not know that Bodhisattvas dwelling in this land also transcribe scriptures, build temples, and perform offerings and acts of charity to adorn the Buddha-field?
Subhūti replied: "No, World-Honored One. Adornment does not exceed external appearances; it has no bearing upon intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). A Bodhisattva certainly would not do so."
This is so. Why is this? For a Buddha-field is itself a pure land (*śuddhakṣetra*). A pure land does not require artificial embellishment;
what is called "ornamentation" is not true ornamentation, but is merely a conventional designation for ornamentation.
Therefore, I instruct you, Subhūti: although the nature and capacity of all bodhisattvas are vast, they should all act in this manner.
One gives rise to a pure mind. What is meant by "pure"? One should not give rise to the mind by dwelling upon that which has form and color;
one should not give rise to the mind by dwelling upon sounds, fragrances, tastes, tangibles, or mental phenomena (*dharma*).
"One should simply eliminate the six sense-objects and give rise to the mind in a state of non-abiding. The Buddha spoke again:
"Subhūti, suppose there were a person whose body was like Sumeru, the king of mountains. What do you think? Would it be large? Subhūti replied:
"It would be very large, World-Honored One. Yet although this body is large, in the final analysis, it is not definitively large."
Why is this? For all things that possess form and appearance belong to the realm of exhaustion.

Even if the physical body were as vast as Mount Sumeru, it would ultimately still be subject to birth and cessation. Only that which accords with what the Buddha described as the "non-body" can be called the "Great Body.
Now, that which is the non-body is the Dharma-body; it is the True Mind. It is capable of encompassing the Great Void.
The world-realm of the *koṭi*—how could it be merely like Sumeru, the king of mountains? Section Eleven:
The Superiority of Unconditioned Merit (Cultivating Unconditioned Merit Surpasses Giving).

Subhūti, suppose there were as many Ganges Rivers as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River; what do you think? [If there were that many Ganges Rivers,] would the grains of sand in them be numerous?
"What do you think? Are all those grains of sand in the Ganges many? Subhūti said, "Very many, World-Honored One.
Those Ganges Rivers alone are already countless, let alone their sands. "Subhūti, I now tell you the truth:
if there were a son of good family or a daughter of good family who filled as many great trichiliocosms as there are grains of sand in those Ganges Rivers with the seven treasures..."
"If one were to give as a gift a thousand worlds, would the merit obtained be great? Subhūti replied, "It would be very great, World-Honored One.

The Buddha told Subhūti, "If a son of good family or a daughter of good family, from within this sutra, were to even receive and uphold a four-line verse or the like and explain it for others, this merit would surpass the former merit."
[Note] The Ganges River is forty *li* in circumference and is located in the Western Regions; it is commonly seen by all people, which is why the Buddha took it as a metaphor.
"Equal" (*deng*) means the same.

[Commentary] This was the eighth section of the preceding [chapter]. It stated that giving the three-thousandfold great thousandfold world-system as an offering of the seven treasures is not equal to upholding this sutra.
The Buddha further expanded upon this meaning, saying: "Subhūti, the Ganges River is forty *li* in circumference; it may be called vast.
The number of grains of sand contained within it is difficult to calculate entirely. If one grain of sand..."
"Suppose each of these rivers were equal in size to the Ganges River. What do you think, Subhūti?
Would the sands of all these Ganges Rivers be numerous? Subhūti replied, "Very numerous, World-Honored One.

Consequently, they are unable to hear, receive, read, recite, or explain this sutra for others, not realizing that this sutra universally delivers all beings.
It is most subtle and most wondrous, Subhūti. Wherever this sūtra exists in any empty place, it is like a maṇi jewel, its auspicious radiance brilliant and dazzling.
All those in the world—whether in the realm of devas, the realm of humans, or the realm of asuras—who encounter it will not fail to make offerings with a sincere heart.
You should know that such a place is equivalent to a repository for the true bodily relics of a Buddha.
Like a precious stūpa, it should be revered by all; one should prostrate, circumambulate it, and scatter various flowers and incense upon that spot.
This refers to cases such as when a single person resolves their mind and the various devas prepare offerings. It is of this nature.
Chapter Sixteen: The Section on Purifying Karmic Obstructions (If one can purify karmic obstructions, they will be entirely eliminated).

Furthermore, Subhūti, if a son of good family or a daughter of good family receives, upholds, reads, and recites this sutra, yet is treated with contempt by others, it is because of their karmic offenses from previous lives which ought to have caused them to fall into the evil realms;
it is because of these [past offenses] that they are now treated with contempt by others in the present life.
The sinful karma of previous lives will be immediately extinguished, and one shall attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Subhūti, I recall that in the past, during immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas before the time of Dīpaṃkara Buddha,
I encountered eight hundred and forty thousand *koṭi-nayuta* Buddhas, all of whom I served and made offerings to, none of whom I failed to honor.

Furthermore, Subhūti, if there should be a son of good family or a daughter of good family who, in the final age at the end of time, is able to receive, uphold, read, and recite this sutra, the merit they obtain shall not be matched by even a hundredth part of the merit from my offerings to all the Buddhas;
nor by a thousandth, ten-thousandth, or a hundred-thousand-millionth part;
indeed, it cannot be reached even by calculation, number, or analogy. Subhūti, if a son of good family or a daughter of good family, in the final age at the end of time...
World-Honored One, if I were to describe in detail the merit obtained by those who receive, uphold, read, and recite this sutra,
some people upon hearing it would immediately become deranged in mind, harboring doubts and failing to believe. Subhūti, you should know that the meaning of this sutra is inconceivable,
and its karmic fruit and retribution are likewise inconceivable.
[Note] "Contempt" refers to being despised by others due to conditions such as illness, poverty, and various signs of decline.
"Evil realms" refers to the hells, hungry ghosts, and animals. The Sanskrit term *asaṃkhyeya* translates into Chinese as "innumerable.
The Sanskrit term *nayuta* translates into Chinese as "ten million. "In full detail" means to speak with thorough precision.
【Commentary】 One who upholds and recites this sutra ought to be revered and made offerings to by devas and humans;
yet, they often cannot avoid being treated with contempt by others. Few do not conclude that such recitation is of no benefit. Therefore, the Buddha said:
"Subhūti, if a son of good family or a daughter of good family receives, upholds, reads, and recites this sutra, and is instead treated with contempt by others, this is..."
In a previous life, one’s karmic offenses were deep and heavy; one ought to have fallen into the three evil realms of hell, hungry ghosts, or animals.
Because of the merit from reciting [this scripture] in this present life, one merely suffers being slighted and despised by others. Such is the retribution for the karmic offenses of former lives.
It shall be immediately extinguished. In a future life, the fruit of Buddhahood—unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment—shall be attained and accomplished.

Subhūti, it is just as I myself, in days past, having passed through immeasurable and incalculable kalpas, encountered eight hundred and forty thousand *koṭi-nayuta* Buddhas before the Buddha Dīpaṃkara, and made offerings to and served them all.
No effort shall go to waste; yet it merely seeks worldly blessings and cannot lead one to transcend the sea of suffering.

However, if there should be someone in the future final age who can receive, uphold, read, and recite this sutra, thereby awakening to their own original nature and forever escaping the cycle of rebirth, the merit they obtain—when compared with the merit I have gained from making offerings to all the Buddhas—is a hundredfold greater.
It cannot equal even one part of it; even when divided into millions, billions, or trillions of parts, or even as numerous as the sands of the Ganges or atoms of dust, it still cannot reach it.
This is because making offerings constitutes the gift of wealth (*āmiṣa-dāna*), and those who receive the retribution for the gift of wealth gradually diminish until they eventually come to an end.
Reciting and upholding [the scriptures] constitutes the gift of Dharma (*dharma-dāna*). Those who receive the Dharma...
The retribution for such giving increases day by day until it culminates in the attainment of Buddhahood.
Thus, how could this sutra be easily heard by ordinary people? Subhūti, if there are good men or good women in the final age at the end of time...
If I were to describe in detail the wondrous merit obtained by those who uphold,
read, and recite this sutra, those of inferior capacity, upon hearing it, would either become mentally deranged, or else harbor doubts and fail to believe,
regarding my words as mere exaggeration and finding them strange. Subhūti, you should know the essential meaning of this sutra.
The fruits and retributions of these merits are all beyond the reach of thought and cannot be discussed even daily;
how then could I possibly provide a full exposition of them?
Chapter Seventeen: Ultimate Non-Self (The ultimate realization of Buddhahood is fundamentally devoid of the mark of self).

At that time, Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, how should a son of good family or a daughter of good family who has resolved to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* abide? How should they subdue their minds? The Buddha told Subhūti:
"Son of good family, daughter of good family, as for those who have resolved to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*..."
One should give rise to this thought: "I should bring all sentient beings to parinirvāṇa.
Yet, after having brought all sentient beings to parinirvāṇa, there is not a single sentient being who has actually been brought to parinirvāṇa. Why is this?
Subhūti, if a bodhisattva possesses the mark of a self, the mark of a person, the mark of a sentient being, or the mark of a life-span, they are not a bodhisattva. For what reason? Subhūti...
Subhūti, truly there is no dharma by which one sets out for anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Subhūti, what do you think? Did the Tathāgata, while in the presence of Dīpaṃkara Buddha, obtain any dharma called anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi?
"No, World-Honored One. As I understand the meaning of what the Buddha has taught, the Buddha [did not obtain any dharma] from Dīpaṃkara Buddha."
There is no dharma by which the Tathāgata has attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. The Buddha said:
"So it is, so it is, Subhūti. Truly, there is no dharma by which the Tathāgata has attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Subhūti, if there were a dharma by which the Tathāgata had attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, then [the Buddha] would have been predicted by Dīpaṃkara..."
The Buddha did not then grant me the prediction: "In a future age, you shall attain Buddhahood and be named Śākyamuni.
This was because there is truly no dharma by which one attains *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. For this reason, Dīpaṃkara Buddha—
"Grant me a prediction," he said. "In a future age, you shall become a Buddha named Śākyamuni. Why is this?

'Tathāgata' means the suchness of all dharmas. If someone were to say that the Tathāgata has attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, Subhūti, in reality there is no dharma by which a Buddha attains *anuttara*..."

“Samyaksambodhi. Subhūti, as for the anuttarasamyaksambodhi attained by the Tathāgata, therein there is neither reality nor unreality. Therefore, the Tathāgata says that all dharmas are the Buddha-dharma.”
Subhūti, that which is called "all dharmas" is itself not all dharmas; therefore it is called "all dharmas.
Subhūti, it is like the body of a person being tall and large. Subhūti said, "World-Honored One, when the Tathāgata speaks of the body of a person being tall and large, it is itself not a large body;
it is called a 'large body' [only] by name. Subhūti, a bodhisattva is also like this. If...
To speak thus, saying, "I shall bring immeasurable sentient beings to final nirvāṇa," is not to be called a bodhisattva.

Why is this? Subhūti, in reality there is no dharma that is named "bodhisattva. Therefore, the Buddha has said that all dharmas are without self, without person, without sentient being, and without life-span. Subhūti, if a bodhisattva were to say, "I shall adorn..."
"Buddha-field. One who does so is not called a bodhisattva. Why? What the Tathāgata calls the adornment of a Buddha-field is itself no adornment;
it is merely designated as 'adornment. Subhūti, if a bodhisattva penetrates the dharma of non-self, the Tathāgata declares him to be a true bodhisattva."
[Note] *Śākya* in Sanskrit; in the language of China, "Capable Benevolent One" (*Néngrén*). *Muni* in Sanskrit; in the language of China, "Silent One" (*Jīmò*).

From the passage beginning with "Because at that time... down to the phrase "In truth, there is no dharma by which one sets forth toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*," although it resembles the third division, the third division speaks of the extinction of all [beings], whereas this refers to those still in life.
Regarding the phrase "such a mind," the statement that "one gives rise to such a mind" is also not ultimately real. While the words are the same, their meanings differ in depth.

This is because, from the passage concerning the Buddha Dīpaṃkara down to the sentence "neither real nor unreal," although it resembles the seventh and fourteenth sections, the seventh section states that while there is no fixed dharma, there is still dharma.
In this context, it is said that there is truly no dharma; thus, both [subject and object] are simultaneously empty.
While the fourteenth section specifically refers to non-attachment to the four marks in relation to giving and patience, this [present section] encompasses all things.

It is therefore felt to be even more profound, subtle, and vast than what preceded it. For this reason, the Tathāgata spoke the following words regarding all dharmas: [The passage continues: "Below this..."
At the conclusion, although it resembles the tenth section, that tenth section does not contain such expressions as "ornament" or "great body," but merely discusses its principles in abstract terms.
This statement, however, speaks of penetrating the dharma of non-self; thus, one may directly ascend to the other shore.
Furthermore, it discusses its efficacy and serves to inspire and guide future students.
[Commentary]: Since this sutra cannot be conceived by the mind nor discussed by the mouth, its reception, retention, reading, and recitation are unavoidable.

At that time, Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, for a son of good family or a daughter of good family who has resolved upon the mind of unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, in what place should this mind abide so that it may be able to subdue [the afflictions]?"

"Is it not delusive thought? The Buddha said to Subhūti, "Good sons and good daughters who have resolved to attain unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment should give rise to a mind that transcends and realizes [the nature of] all sentient beings.
They should lift up all sentient beings, completely extinguishing their delusive thoughts and delivering them. They should bring all sentient beings to parinirvāṇa until none remain."
I have already attained Buddhahood, yet there is not a single sentient being who has truly entered parinirvāṇa. This is because sentient beings extinguish themselves and deliver themselves;
I have no merit in this. Why is this so? It is because to harbor the thought of "attaining parinirvāṇa" is itself to be attached to signs (*nimitta*).
If the mind of a Bodhisattva is attached to even a single sign, then there is the self, the person, the sentient being, and the life-span.
Such a view is that of one who is not yet a Bodhisattva. Since there is no mark to which one can become attached, there is no dharma that can be named.

Not only are external sensory conditions entirely empty and void, but even that which is called "giving rise to the mind of unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment" is inherently possessed within our own nature;
how could it be a matter of following established paths or adhering to dharmas?
"How wonderful! Let me ask you this: when I was formerly with the Buddha Dīpaṃkara, I received many predictions that I would attain unsurpassed bodhi.
Do you think there is any fixed dharma therein? Subhūti replied, "No."

“World-Honored One, as I understand the meaning of what the Buddha has taught, since all things are empty, one knows that at the place of the Buddha Dīpaṃkara, there was no dharma by which supreme enlightenment was attained. The Buddha, deeply affirming these words, said:
“So it is, so it is, Subhūti. Truly, there is no dharma by which a Tathāgata attains supreme enlightenment. If...”
If there were a fixed dharma for attaining unsurpassed bodhi, then Dīpaṃkara Buddha would not have granted me a prediction;
he would have immediately transmitted to me the method for becoming a Buddha.
Why then would he have repeatedly said to me, "In a future life, you shall become a Buddha named Śākyamuni"? Truly, there is nothing of the sort.
Because he attained unsurpassed bodhi through the Dharma, Dīpaṃkara Buddha bestowed upon me a prediction, saying:
"In a future age, you shall become a Buddha named Śākyamuni," and so forth. Now, this prediction is the wondrous truth of the Tathāgata’s attainment of the fruit;
and the Tathāgata is none other than true nature (*tathatā*). This true nature penetrates the three [times].
The world extends throughout the ten directions; this is the meaning that all phenomena attain their own suchness. How could there be any fixed dharma to be named?
If someone were to say, "When the Tathāgata attains unsurpassed bodhi, there must necessarily be a fixed dharma," these are all false words and are not to be trusted.
How could one know that the Tathāgata’s attainment of unsurpassed bodhi is anything other than [the realization of]...?
Through the long accumulation of merit and the gradual cultivation of practice, one attains the subtle mastery of mind and spirit.
As all conditions are purified and all phenomena are empty, there is truly no dharma to be attained. Yet, while there is no dharma to be attained, it cannot be said that there is no attainment.
Within this attainment of non-attainment, there is reality yet not reality; there is emptiness yet not emptiness. Thus, the Tathāgata...
I have always taught that all dharmas are the means by which one practices to achieve Buddhahood.
To employ them for practice is to be empty yet not empty; yet achieving Buddhahood does not originally reside therein, for it is real yet not real.
How could one possibly adhere rigidly to this? Subhūti, regarding all that the Tathāgata has spoken—
The Dharma is not any truly real dharma; it is merely by relying on these provisional designations that one practices, and thus they are called "all dharmas" as empty names.
This meaning can be understood through an analogy. Subhūti, it is like a person whose body is tall and large.
"Is this truly so? Subhūti replied, "World-Honored One, although the Tathāgata speaks of a body that is vast and great, it still possesses arising and ceasing and is subject to limitation;
it is not a truly real great body, but is merely called a 'great body' by way of conventional designation."
The Buddha said, "Subhūti, when a bodhisattva teaches and transforms sentient beings, it is not for the sake of reality; it is like the unreality of a 'great body.

If a bodhisattva were to say, 'I have brought immeasurable sentient beings to parinirvāṇa,' one should know that such a view and consciousness are the very factors for attaining Buddhahood. Even so, it may still be called 'bodhi' (awakening)."
Is it so? Why is this? It is because the true nature is empty and void; there is not even a single dharma that is real.
Even the name "Bodhisattva" belongs to the realm of the false and provisional. In reality, there is no such thing as a dharma called a "Bodhisattva.
Therefore, the Buddha taught that all dharmas are devoid of self, person, sentient being, or life-span. Since these four do not exist, how could there be anything else?

This refers to the Bodhisattva. When one reaches the state of transcending marks (*lakṣaṇa*) to deliver sentient beings, causing all worlds to become pure—this is precisely the locus of true adornment.

If a Bodhisattva does not seek it in this way, but instead says, "I shall adorn the worldly Buddha-fields with gold, pearls, and other jewels," they merely possess the views of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*). It is not so.
One is named a Bodhisattva. Why is this? When the Tathāgata speaks of adorning Buddha-lands, it refers to nothing more than external adornments;
these are not true adornments, but are merely designated as such by convention.
One who gives rise to a mind of deliverance while remaining attached to the signs of adornment cannot be called a Bodhisattva. Ultimately, what kind of mind must one arouse [to be so named]?

Can one be called a bodhisattva? It is necessary that one be thoroughly proficient in all directions, deeply clarifying the dharma of non-self, remaining far removed from all marks, and forgetting both person and phenomena;
only then do the mind of deliverance and the mind of adornment [truly arise].
Neither arises. Therefore, the Tathāgata calls him a true Bodhisattva. Section XVIII:
On the Single Essence and Identical Contemplation (The Ten Thousand Dharmas Return to One; There is No Further Diverse Contemplation). Subhūti, what do you think?
Does the Tathāgata possess the fleshly eye? "Yes, World-Honored One, the Tathāgata possesses [the fleshly eye]."
"Subhūti, what do you think? Does the Tathāgata possess the divine eye? "Yes, World-Honored One, the Tathāgata possesses the divine eye.
"Subhūti, what do you think? Does the Tathāgata possess the wisdom-eye?
"Yes, World-Honored One, the Tathāgata possesses the wisdom-eye. "Subhūti, what do you think? Does the Tathāgata possess the Dharma-eye? "Yes..."
"Yes, World-Honored One. The Tathāgata possesses the Dharma-eye. "Subhūti, what do you think? Does the Tathāgata possess the Buddha-eye?
"Yes, World-Honored One. The Tathāgata possesses the Buddha-eye. "Subhūti, what do you think?
Regarding all the sands in the Ganges River, does the Buddha say they are sand? "Yes, World-Honored One. The Tathāgata says they are sand. Subhūti...

“Ānanda, what do you think? Suppose there were as many Ganges Rivers as there are grains of sand in one Ganges River, and then as many Buddha-worlds as there are grains of sand in all those Ganges Rivers—would they be many?
“Very many, World-Honored One. The Buddha told Subhūti: “In all those lands, however many kinds of minds there are among all sentient beings...”
They will all know them. Why is this? The Tathāgata has taught that all minds are non-minds; it is for this reason they are called "minds.
And why is this, Subhūti? Because the past mind cannot be apprehended, the present mind cannot be apprehended, and the future mind cannot be apprehended.
[Note] To see the forms and colors of sentient beings is called the flesh eye (*māṃsa-cakṣus*). To see the great trichiliocosm is called the heavenly eye (*divya-cakṣus*).
To see the *prajñā* of one's own nature is called the wisdom eye (*prajñā-cakṣus*). To see that all phenomena (*dharma*) are the absence of all phenomena is called the Dharma eye (*dharma-cakṣus*).
There is no self-nature to be maintained, and there are no Buddhas to be sought. One emits a great radiance that shatters all darkness.
"Darkness" is named the Buddha-eye. Thus it is, World-Honored One; such being the case, he further designates it as follows: "If" means "as it is.
"Gan" means "number," referring to the various distinctions within the minds of sentient beings. "Non-mind" refers to the mind of false conceptualization; when this is absent, it is called "mind.
Not giving rise to false conceptualization is precisely the original mind. This applies to the past and the present.
The future is called one of the three periods of time; it is "unobtainable," which means it cannot exist.
[Commentary] It was stated above that one must penetrate the dharma of non-self before one can be called a Bodhisattva.
Nevertheless, within true emptiness, there exists a genuine vision. Therefore, the Buddha said: "Subhūti, what do you think? Does the Tathāgata have a view?"
"Do you see the fleshly eyes of sentient beings? Subhūti replied, "It is so, World-Honored One;
the Tathāgata possesses fleshly eyes. The Buddha said, "Subhūti, what do you think? Does the Tathāgata possess the divine eye that universally illumines the world?
Subhūti replied, "It is so, World-Honored One; the Tathāgata possesses the divine eye. The Buddha said, "Subhūti..."
"Subhūti, what do you think? Does the Tathāgata possess the eye of wisdom that looks back and illuminates within?
Subhūti replied, "So it is, World-Honored One; the Tathāgata possesses the eye of wisdom. The Buddha said, "Subhūti, what do you think?"
“Does the Tathāgata possess the Dharma-eye that perceives all phenomena as empty? Subhūti replied, “It is so, World-Honored One;
the Tathāgata possesses the Dharma-eye. The Buddha said, “Subhūti, what do you think?
Does the Tathāgata possess the Buddha-eye, whose true nature is eternally luminous, reaching upward to the heavens and downward to the nine depths of darkness, without the slightest obstruction?”
Subhūti said, “So it is, World-Honored One. The Tathāgata possesses the Buddha-eye.
Since the Buddha is endowed with these five eyes, his knowledge is infinitely vast; how could there be anything he does not perceive regarding the minds of all sentient beings?
Therefore, the Buddha spoke again: “Subhūti, what do you think? As for all the grains of sand in the Ganges River, the Buddha has spoken of them...”
“Is that so, Subhūti? Subhūti replied, “It is so, World-Honored One; the Tathāgata has said they are grains of sand.

The Buddha said, “Subhūti, what do you think? Suppose all the grains of sand in a single Ganges River were each divided to become a separate Ganges River, and all the grains of sand within those various Ganges Rivers were each divided to become a separate Buddha-world.”
"Buddha-worlds are thus. Would they not be many? Subhūti replied, "Very many, World-Honored One.
The Buddha said, "Subhūti, although those Buddha-worlds are many, there are all the various kinds of minds belonging to all sentient beings therein."
These are collectively termed the deluded mind. The Tathāgata is fully able to know them all, for the essence of nature is luminous and its light shines everywhere without exception.
That which shines everywhere without exception is the eternally abiding true mind, which remains unchanged throughout ten thousand kalpas.
Why is this? The Tathāgata says that all minds are collectively false and illusory; they are all "not-mind."
If one realizes that all minds are not mind, this is called "mind. Furthermore, how could there be the delusive thoughts of past, present, and future?
Why is this so? Subhūti, whatever thought recalls a prior event is the past mind;
whatever thought attends to a present event is the present mind; whatever thought anticipates a future event is the future mind. These three—
The three kinds of mind originally do not exist; they arise only due to circumstances. Now, since the true mind abides eternally, the myriad dharmas are turned away from emptiness.
How, then, could these three kinds of mind exist?
Chapter Nineteen: The Universal Transformation of the Dharma Realm (The Dharmakāya Pervades the Realm and Universally Transforms Boundlessly).

Subhūti, what do you think? If someone were to fill a trichiliocosm with the seven treasures and give them as a gift, would that person, by reason of this, acquire much merit? “It would be so, World-Honored One; that person would [acquire much merit].”
For this reason, the merit obtained is exceedingly great. Subhūti, if merit were substantial, the Tathāgata would not say that one obtains much merit;
because merit is non-existent, the Tathāgata says that one obtains much merit.
[Note] "Causes and conditions" (hetu-pratyaya) refers to the causal basis. "Possessing actual merit" means that one regards merit as existing and thus gives rise to vain expectations.
"Lacking merit" means that one regards merit as non-existent and thus does not cling to any marks (lakṣaṇa).
This is similar to the eighth section; however, while the eighth section speaks of the giving of the seven treasures, [this section does not].
As for "upholding the sutra," this refers to a person who relies on the sutra to practice giving; this refers to the giving of the seven treasures, whose merit is limited.
This refers to a person who practices giving while remaining detached from signs (*animitta*); compared to the eighth part [of the merit], it appears even more vast and expansive.
【Lecture】 When the mind has an object of attachment, it is no longer the true mind.
It can be seen, therefore, that one should not cling to merit and give rise to expectations. Thus the Buddha said: "Subhūti, what do you think?
If someone were to fill the three-thousandfold world system with the seven treasures and offer them as a gift, would that person, by reason of this act of giving, obtain [much merit]?"
"Is the merit not great? Subhūti replied, "It is so, World-Honored One. By such causes and conditions, this person obtains very great merit.
The Buddha said, "To cultivate the cause and obtain the fruit is the constant law of retribution.
That one who gives the seven treasures obtains very great merit is indeed the natural principle. However, those of the Lesser Vehicle regard merit as something existent and rely upon giving..."
To pursue one's private interests is the merit of a deluded mind; though it may be great, it ultimately belongs to the realm of minor fruits and cannot escape exhaustion.
Therefore, the Tathāgata does not say that such merit is great.
Only those of great wisdom regard merit as non-existent, relying on giving to cultivate their own nature. This is the merit obtained through the Buddha-mind. It is, for example, like...
Since space has no boundaries, the Tathāgata says that the merit obtained is vast.
How could that which is given while clinging to signs ever be compared to this?
Chapter Twenty: Detachment from Form and Characteristics (Form and characteristics are all delusive;
by detaching from delusion, one sees the nature). Subhūti, what do you think? Can the Buddha be seen by means of his complete physical body (*rūpakāya*)? “No, World-Honored One.”
One should not perceive the Tathāgata by means of the perfection of the physical body (*rūpakāya*). Why is this?

What the Tathāgata calls the perfection of the physical body is itself not the perfection of the physical body; it is merely designated as the "perfection of the physical body. Subhūti, what do you think?
Can the Tathāgata be perceived by means of the perfection of the various marks (*lakṣaṇa*)? "No, World-Honored One. The Tathāgata should not be perceived by means of the perfection..."
[The Tathāgata] perceives all marks. Why is this? The Tathāgata’s possession of all marks is itself not a possession;
it is called the possession of all marks. [Note: "Possession" means being without any deficiency. The "form-body" refers to the thirty-two marks. He possesses all these marks.
The supernormal power of transformation does not stop at the thirty-two marks alone. This is similar to the fifth and thirteenth sections;

however, while the fifth section states that all marks whatsoever are empty and false—intending for people to see the markless Tathāgata within the Tathāgata who possesses marks—this [passage] speaks of being "endowed with form."
The body. Furthermore, it says that one who possesses all the marks sees the Tathāgata of fixed true nature within the Tathāgata who is wondrous and unfathomable.
The thirteenth section states: "Rather than seeing the Tathāgata’s thirty-two marks as a mere conventionality, it is better to uphold the Sūtra as the reality.
This statement is intended to lead people to uphold the Sūtra; this is not only... [text ends]
The thirty-two marks are provisional; even the supernormal powers of transformation are not real. This is the ultimate praise of the Tathāgata;
though the words are the same, the meaning is inherently different.
【Lecture】 Introduction: That which all Buddhas realize is unconditioned merit (*asaṃskṛta-puṇya*).
How, then, could there be any physical form (*rūpa-kāya*) to be perceived? Therefore, the Buddha said: "Subhūti, what do you think?
Can the Buddha be seen by means of a physical body endowed with the thirty-two marks? Subhūti replied: "No, World-Honored One. All physical bodies..."
